name: Jonang (jo nang pa)
alt_names: the Great Madhyamaka (dbu ma chen po) of Dolpopa
regions: Jomonang valley in Tsang, central Tibet (the Jonang monastery and its great stūpa)
Takten Phuntsok Ling (rtag brtan phun tshogs gling) in Tsang, Tāranātha's seat
Dzamthang ('dzam thang) and the Amdo/Gyalrong/Golok borderlands (the surviving tradition)
Mongolia (Tāranātha's activity; the Jebtsundamba line counted as his rebirth)

tradition.text: Kālacakra received from Śambhala through the Indian masters and the Kashmiri Somanātha (11th c.); the Jonang hermitage founded by Künpang Thukje Tsöndrü; the view of other-emptiness taught openly by Dolpopa (1292–1361), who holds it to be the teaching of the age of perfection

scholarly.text: Jonang hermitage founded c. 1294; Dolpopa's zhentong formulated c. 1320s–1330s; Tāranātha 1575–1634; Tsang seats converted to Gelug c. 1650–1658; continues in Amdo to the present

transmissions_received.what: the Kālacakra tantra, the Vimalaprabhā and the six-branch vajra-yoga (chiefly the Dro lineage from Somanātha; Künpang Thukje Tsöndrü is said to have gathered seventeen lineages of the six-branch yoga)
the tathāgatagarbha sūtras and the Ratnagotravibhāga, read as definitive teaching of an ultimate empty of what is other than it
the Maitreya texts and the three natures, read as Great Madhyamaka
Dolpopa's early training (Sakya monastery) before he took charge of Jonang
the Shangpa instructions held by Tāranātha
the seven instruction lineages (bka' babs bdun ldan) received by Tāranātha from the Indian yogin Buddhaguptanātha

transmissions_given.what: the other-emptiness view (through Jamgön Kongtrul's Great Madhyamaka) and the Kālacakra six-branch yoga counted as one of the eight great practice lineages
a shentong strand of buddha-nature interpretation (8th Situ, Jamgön Kongtrul), contested within the school
the Tsang seats and their communities, converted in the mid-17th c.
a revised Tibetan translation of the Kālacakra and Vimalaprabhā made under Dolpopa by Jonang Lotsawa Lodrö Pal and Mati Paṇchen (the 'Jonang translation')

distinctive_positions: Two truths: conventional phenomena are empty of their own nature (rang stong); the ultimate — the dharmatā, dharmakāya, buddha-nature — is empty only of what is other than it (gzhan stong), i.e. of the adventitious conventional phenomena, and is not empty of its own nature and qualities.
The ultimate is permanent, stable, peaceful and eternal (rtag brtan ther zug g.yung drung) and is not a dependent arising.
Buddha-nature is present in all beings complete with the buddha-qualities, which are uncovered, not newly produced (Ratnagotravibhāga 1.154-155 read literally).

The third turning (the tathāgatagarbha sūtras and the Maitreya texts), the Kālacakra and the 'bodhisattva commentaries', and Nāgārjuna's hymns (the Dharmadhātustava) teach the definitive meaning; together they are the Great Madhyamaka (dbu ma chen po).
The ālaya is twofold: the ālaya-consciousness (kun gzhi rnam shes), which is conventional, and the ālaya-wisdom (kun gzhi ye shes), which is ultimate.
Dolpopa presents his teaching as the doctrine of the age of perfection (rdzogs ldan, kṛtayuga), a 'fourth council' restoring the Buddha's final intent.
The Kālacakra six-branch vajra-yoga is the principal practice through which the other-empty ultimate — 'the emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects' — is directly realized.
summary: A Tibetan school centred on the Kālacakra tantra and on the view of 'other-emptiness' (gzhan stong). Its Kālacakra lineage runs from the 11th-century master Yumo Mikyö Dorje; the Jonang hermitage was founded by Künpang Thukje Tsöndrü (c. 1294). Dolpopa Sherab Gyaltsen (1292–1361) taught openly that the ultimate — buddha-nature, the dharmakāya — is permanent and empty only of adventitious phenomena other than itself, in his Mountain Doctrine and Fourth Council, and oversaw a new translation of the Kālacakra. Tāranātha (1575–1634) revived the school, wrote on other-emptiness, on Kālacakra practice and on the history of Buddhism in India. In the mid-17th century its Tsang seats were converted to Gelug and its writings restricted under the Fifth Dalai Lama's government; the tradition survived in Amdo (Dzamthang), and its view was revived more widely by the 19th-century Rimé masters.
notes: Historical metadata (scholarly account): the conversion of Takten Phuntsok Ling (renamed Ganden Phuntsok Ling) and the sealing of Jonang printing blocks are usually dated c. 1650–1658, after Tāranātha's death; the reasons given in the sources are both doctrinal and political (Tāranātha's patrons were the Tsang rulers defeated in 1642). Exact years: moderate confidence.

name: Chöd (gcod), 'Cutting'
alt_names: gcod yul ('the object to be cut')
Mahāmudrā Chöd (phyag rgya chen po gcod yul)
the Chöd of the Perfection of Wisdom (shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i gcod)
regions: Central and southern Tibet (Zangri Khangmar, Machig's seat, in Lhokha)
all Tibetan regions through wandering Chöd practitioners (gcod pa)

tradition.text: Machig Labdrön, an emanation of the Great Mother Prajñāpāramitā, receives the teaching from Padampa Sangye, from her teacher Kyotön Sönam Lama and directly in visions; the only Dharma said to have gone from Tibet to India

scholarly.text: late 11th – early 12th c. (Machig's dates are given variously: 1055–1149, 1031–1129 and others); integrated into all Tibetan schools from the 13th–14th c.

transmissions_received.what: the 'father lineage' of Chöd and the Prajñāpāramitā instructions of Padampa Sangye
the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras, which Machig recited professionally before her realization
the Vajrayoginī/Tröma Nagmo deity practice, transference (phowa) and feast (gaṇacakra) forms

transmissions_given.what: Chöd liturgies and instructions (from the Third Karmapa Rangjung Dorje)
Chöd within the Longchen Nyingthig (Jigme Lingpa's Laughter of the Ḍākinīs) and the kusāli's accumulation of the preliminaries
Shije and Chöd counted together as one of the eight great practice lineages (Kongtrul's Treasury of Instructions)

distinctive_positions: What is cut (gcod) is ego-clinging (bdag 'dzin), the root of the mind's afflictions; cutting it cuts all four māras.

The four māras of Chöd — the obstructive (thogs bcas), the unobstructive (thogs med), the māra of elation (dga' brod) and the māra of conceit (snyems byed) — are all contained in the last, the self-fixation.
Gods and demons (lha 'dre) are the play of one's own mind; as long as there is ego-clinging there are demons, and when it is cut there are none.

The body, the object of the strongest attachment, is offered in visualization as food to four kinds of guests (the Three Jewels, the protectors, the six classes of beings, and harmful spirits and karmic creditors) — generosity joined with the view of emptiness.
Practice is done in frightening places — charnel grounds, haunted sites (gnyan sa) — so that fear itself exposes and cuts self-grasping.
Its view is the Perfection of Wisdom; Chöd presents itself as the practical application of the Prajñāpāramitā, combining sūtra and mantra.
The tradition's account holds that Chöd is the only Dharma that went from Tibet to India: Indian scholars who came to test Machig accepted her teaching and carried it back.
summary: The practice tradition of 'cutting' ego-clinging founded by the Tibetan woman master Machig Labdrön (11th–12th c.), drawing on the Perfection of Wisdom and on instructions from the Indian siddha Padampa Sangye. It is known for its visualized offering of one's own body to guests of four kinds and for practice in charnel grounds and haunted places, accompanied by drum and thighbone trumpet. It never formed a separate monastic school but entered every Tibetan tradition; the Rimé masters counted Shije and Chöd as one of the eight great practice lineages.
notes: Restricted content: the body-offering is recorded here only as summary with the tradition's own warnings (see prc:chod).

name: Shije (zhi byed), 'Pacification [of suffering]'
regions: later only within other schools' collections

tradition.text: brought by the South Indian siddha Padampa Sangye on several visits to Tibet, his last and longest at Dingri, where he died

scholarly.text: late 11th – early 12th c. (Padampa d. c. 1105 or 1117); transmitted as the early, middle and later lines; no longer an independent institution after c. 15th c.

transmissions_received.what: the siddha instructions Padampa is said to have received from many Indian masters
the Perfection of Wisdom, above all the Heart Sūtra's 'mantra that pacifies all suffering', from which the name is taken

transmissions_given.what: the father lineage of Chöd and Padampa's instructions to Machig Labdrön
counted with Chöd as one of the eight great practice lineages; its instructions gathered in the Treasury of Instructions

distinctive_positions: Suffering is pacified by the realization of the emptiness taught in the Perfection of Wisdom; the name comes from the Heart Sūtra's description of the mantra of wisdom as 'pacifying all suffering'.
Sūtra and mantra instructions are combined and given according to the disciple's capacity.
Renunciation of worldly concerns, solitary practice and devotion to the guru are urged in the plain verses of the Dingri Hundred.
The teaching was given in three transmissions (early, middle, later) on Padampa's successive visits.
summary: The 'Pacification' tradition brought to Tibet by the South Indian siddha Padampa Sangye (d. c. 1105/1117), who taught at Dingri. Grounded in the Perfection of Wisdom — whose mantra 'pacifies all suffering' — it combined sūtra and tantra instructions and was passed down in early, middle and later transmissions, the last through Dampa Kunga. Padampa's Hundred Verses to the people of Dingri remain widely read. As an independent line it faded; its instructions survive in other schools and in Kongtrul's Treasury of Instructions, where it is paired with Chöd.

name: Sowa Rigpa (gso ba rig pa), the Tibetan science of healing
alt_names: gso ba rig pa ('the science of healing')
the medicine of the Four Tantras (rgyud bzhi)
regions: Tibet (Chakpori medical college, Lhasa, 1696; Mentsikhang, Lhasa, 1916)

tradition.text: taught by the Medicine Buddha in the city of Tanaduk; the Four Tantras brought to Tibet and translated by Vairocana in the 8th c., given to Yuthok the Elder (trad. 708–833), hidden at Samye and recovered as treasure by Drapa Ngönshé in 1038

scholarly.text: the Four Tantras compiled in the 12th c. by Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger (1126–1202), with the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya as a principal source; the Jangpa and Zurkharpa schools 15th c.; standardized by Desi Sangye Gyatso 1680s–1703; living

transmissions_received.what: the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (Tibetan translation in the Tengyur's medical section, with its commentaries) — the eight branches, the three doṣas, seven dhātus, six tastes, daily and seasonal regimen
the Medicine Buddha as teacher, the tantra form of the Four Tantras, consecration of medicines and the physician's deity practice (Yuthok Nyingthig)
the Bhaiṣajyaguru sūtra and the doctrine that ignorance and the three poisons are the root of all disease

transmissions_given.what: medicine counted among the sciences in Kongtrul's Treasury of Knowledge (as recalled; low confidence)

distinctive_positions: The Four Tantras were taught by the Medicine Buddha, emanating as the sage Rigpé Yeshe, in answer to the sage Yilé Kyé (the tradition's account).

The ultimate cause of all disease is ignorance (ma rig pa) that does not understand selflessness; from it arise desire, hatred and delusion, which give rise to the three nyepa — rlung, mkhris pa and bad kan.
Health is the balance of the three nyepa, the seven bodily constituents and the three excretions; disease is their imbalance.
Diagnosis is by seeing (above all tongue and urine), touching (above all the pulse) and questioning; treatment is by diet, behaviour, medicines and external therapies, in that order of gentleness.
The whole science is summarized in the image of three trees with roots, trunks, branches and leaves, whose flowers are health and long life and whose fruits are Dharma, wealth and happiness.
The physician must have compassion (bodhicitta) as well as learning; medicine is practised as a path of the bodhisattva.
Some diseases are karmic or caused by spirits (gdon) and need Dharma practice or ritual rather than medicine alone.
summary: The Tibetan science of healing (one of the five major sciences), based on the Four Tantras (rgyud bzhi) — in the tradition's account the word of the Medicine Buddha, in the scholarly account a 12th-century compilation by Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger drawing heavily on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya. It explains health and disease through the three nyepa (rlung, mkhris pa, bad kan), which arise from the three poisons rooted in ignorance, and the seven bodily constituents; it diagnoses by pulse and urine and treats by diet, behaviour, medicines and external therapies. Desi Sangye Gyatso's Blue Beryl commentary and the medical paintings (late 17th c.) fixed the classical tradition, which is practised across the Himalaya, Mongolia and the diaspora.
notes: family 'shared': Buddhist in frame (Medicine Buddha, three poisons), Āyurvedic in much of its content, and also used by Bön physicians with their own origin account (not covered here). Decision in REPORT.

name: Jangpa (byang lugs), the Northern school of Tibetan medicine
distinctive_positions: One of the two classical commentarial schools on the Four Tantras; its readings were weighed against the Zur school in Desi Sangye Gyatso's standardization.
summary: The 'Northern' school of commentary and practice on the Four Tantras associated with the lord of Jang, Namgyal Drakzang (15th c.). Details of its distinctive doctrines are not recalled with confidence.

name: Zurkharpa (zur lugs), the Zur school of Tibetan medicine

scholarly.text: 15th–16th c. (Zurkhar Nyamnyi Dorje 1439–1475; Zurkhar Lodrö Gyalpo 1509–1579)

distinctive_positions: Its commentary, the Oral Instructions of the Ancestors (mes po'i zhal lung), became a principal reference behind the Blue Beryl; Zurkhar Lodrö Gyalpo discussed whether the Four Tantras is the Buddha's word.
summary: The southern commentarial school on the Four Tantras founded by Zurkhar Nyamnyi Dorje and continued by Zurkhar Lodrö Gyalpo, whose commentary shaped later classical medicine.

name: Rimé (ris med), the non-sectarian movement
alt_names: phyogs med ris med ('impartial and non-sectarian')
regions: Kham, above all Derge (Dzongsar, Palpung, Shechen, Dzogchen, Kathok)

tradition.text: not a new school but the renewal of all lineages; its masters are regarded as emanations (Khyentse Wangpo of Jigme Lingpa, Kongtrul of Vairocana)

scholarly.text: c. 1840s–1910s, centred on Derge; continued by 20th-c. teachers

transmissions_received.what: the treasure (terma) cycles and Dzogchen
Marpa Kagyu Mahāmudrā and the Six Yogas
the Shangpa instructions revived by Kongtrul
the Path and Result (Lamdre) and the tantra collections compiled by Loter Wangpo
the Kadam instructions and mind training
the Kālacakra six-branch yoga and the other-emptiness (Great Madhyamaka) view
Chöd, paired with Shije
the Pacification instructions

distinctive_positions: All authentic lineages are to be respected and preserved; disparaging another tradition is the grave fault of abandoning the Dharma.

The whole of Tibetan practice is mapped as eight great chariots of practice lineages: Nyingma, Kadam, Sakya Lamdre, Marpa Kagyu, Shangpa Kagyu, Shije-and-Chöd, the Kālacakra six-branch yoga, and Orgyenpa's approach-and-accomplishment of the three vajras.
Each lineage is to be received, practised and taught in its own terms, without mixing its methods or views with another's.
Rare and endangered transmissions are to be gathered and printed so that they survive (the Five Treasuries; the Compendium of Sādhanas; the Compendium of Tantras).

In Kongtrul's presentation, the other-emptiness Great Madhyamaka and the self-emptiness Madhyamaka each have their place; Mipham defends a Madhyamaka of the unity of appearance and emptiness; the movement does not impose one view.
summary: The 19th-century non-sectarian (ris med) movement of eastern Tibet led by Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo (1820–1892) and Jamgön Kongtrul Lodrö Thayé (1813–1899), with Chokgyur Lingpa, Mipham and Patrul Rinpoche. It gathered, practised and printed the teachings of all Tibetan lineages — above all those in danger of loss — in collections such as Kongtrul's Five Treasuries, organizing them as the eight great practice lineages, and urged respect for every tradition in its own terms. Flagged as recent (post-1800).
notes: The tradition itself presents Rimé as an attitude and a programme of preservation, not as a new school; lineage membership stays with the teachers' own schools.
